advance_directive_requirements: Massachusetts has no living-will statute; the health care proxy under MGL c. 201D is the only advance directive authorized by statute. It must be signed in front of two adult witnesses, who also sign; the named agent cannot be a witness, and no notary is required.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may accept or refuse any health care, including life-prolonging treatment, nutrition and hydration, and may receive palliative care and hospice care. A health care agent may refuse treatment on the person's behalf once capacity is lost.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Massachusetts. MGL c. 201D, § 12 states nothing in that chapter shall be construed to constitute, condone, authorize, or approve suicide or mercy killing. The End of Life Options Act (S. 1486, 2025-2026) is a pending bill and is not law.
notes: No official Massachusetts health care proxy form URL was verified in this research, so advance_directive_url is null; the form is published by the state and by the Massachusetts Medical Society. No bar-referral phone was found on an official page loaded, so help_phone is null.
polst_name: MOLST (Massachusetts Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: MOLST is a clinician-signed medical order for seriously ill or frail patients, based on the patient's decisions about life-sustaining treatments. It is voluntary, takes effect immediately, and does not replace a health care proxy.
proxy_how: Name an adult agent in a written Health Care Proxy under MGL c. 201D. The agent makes health care decisions only after a physician determines in writing that the person lacks capacity, and must follow the person's known wishes.
proxy_name: Health care agent (named in a Health Care Proxy)

advance_directive_requirements: Michigan has no living-will statute; the operative document is the Patient Advocate Designation under MCL 700.5506 et seq. It must be signed in front of two witnesses, and the named patient advocate must sign an acceptance before acting. No notary is required.
hospice_refusal: A person may refuse or stop life-sustaining treatment, and a patient advocate may do so on their behalf under the limits above. Withholding or withdrawing medical treatment is expressly excluded from the criminal assistance to suicide statute.
maid_prohibited_note: Michigan has no medical aid in dying law. Under MCL 750.329a, knowingly assisting another person to end their life is a felony punishable by up to five years in prison, a fine of up to $10,000, or both. Senate Bill 681 (2023), the proposed Michigan Death with Dignity Act, stalled in committee and did not become law.
notes: No bar-referral phone was found on an official page loaded, so help_phone is null. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services also offers a separate advance directive for mental health care.
polst_name: MI-POST (Michigan Physician Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: MI-POST is an optional medical order for adults with advanced illness or frailty, created by Public Act 154 of 2017. It records decisions about CPR, critical care, and end-of-life goals, is signed by the patient or representative and a clinician, and does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Name a patient advocate in a written Patient Advocate Designation. The advocate may make care, custody, and medical treatment decisions, including withholding or withdrawing life-prolonging treatment, only when the person cannot participate in decisions, and only if the person stated in a clear and convincing manner that the advocate may allow death.

advance_directive_requirements: Under Minn. Stat. § 145C.03, a health care directive must be in writing, dated, and signed, and the signature must be verified by a notary public or by two witnesses. The health care agent cannot act as a witness or notary for the directive.
hospice_refusal: A person may give health care instructions refusing treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, and providers must honor those wishes or transfer the person to a provider who will. Hospice and palliative care are available as comfort-focused care for serious illness.
maid_prohibited_note: Minnesota has no medical aid in dying law. Minn. Stat. § 609.215 prohibits aiding suicide, and Minn. Stat. ch. 145C states that no health care directive may override that prohibition. The End-of-Life Option Act (HF 1930 in 2023-2024; SF 3215 / HF 2998 in 2025-2026) did not advance out of committee.
notes: The Minnesota Department of Health page directs people to free health care directives from their local health care provider or system and to LawHelpMN. No bar-referral phone was found on an official page loaded, so help_phone is null.
polst_note: Minnesota POLST is a provider's medical order, signed by a health care provider, that tells first responders what treatments a seriously ill person wants in an emergency. It works alongside a health care directive and does not replace it.
proxy_how: Appoint a health care agent in the health care directive, under Minn. Stat. ch. 145C. The agent may make any health care decisions the person could make, including decisions about life-prolonging care, when a physician determines the person cannot make decisions.

advance_directive_requirements: Under Miss. Code Ann. §§ 41-41-201 to 41-41-229, with the optional form at § 41-41-209, the directive must be signed by two qualified adult witnesses who know the person, or acknowledged before a notary public in Mississippi. A witness cannot be the agent, a health care provider, or an employee of a health care provider or facility.
hospice_refusal: A person may give instructions to provide, withhold, or withdraw treatment to keep them alive, including artificial nutrition and hydration, and may direct that pain relief be provided at all times even if it hastens death. Hospice care is available as comfort-focused care for terminal illness.
maid_prohibited_note: Mississippi has no medical aid in dying law, and no authorizing statute was found. No prohibiting statute was verified from an official source in this research, so maid_law is null.
notes: Mississippi's POLST is also called a Physician Order Regarding Sustaining Treatment (POST) in some sources. No official state-agency form URL or bar-referral phone was verified in this research, so help_phone is null.
polst_note: Mississippi law at Miss. Code Ann. § 41-41-302 provides for a POLST, a medical order recording a patient's wishes for life-sustaining treatment in their current state of health. It is voluntary, is usually for people with advanced illness, and does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Name an agent in Part 1 of the Advance Health-Care Directive. Unless the form limits the agent, the agent may make all health care decisions, including consenting to or refusing care and directing the withholding or withdrawal of artificial nutrition and hydration.
proxy_name: Agent (power of attorney for health care)

advance_directive_name: Missouri Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care and Health Care Directive (living will declaration)
advance_directive_requirements: The Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care under RSMo §§ 404.800 to 404.872 must be acknowledged before a notary public. The living will declaration under RSMo §§ 459.010 to 459.055, with a sample form at § 459.015, must be signed in front of two adult witnesses.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse or stop treatment, including death-prolonging procedures, through a health care directive. Missouri's living will statute excludes nutrition and hydration from the death-prolonging procedures that can be refused under that statute. Hospice care is available as comfort-focused care.
maid_prohibited_note: Missouri has no medical aid in dying law, and no authorizing statute was found. No prohibiting statute was verified from an official source in this research, so maid_law is null.
notes: The Missouri Bar publishes a free combined Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care and Health Care Directive form, but its direct URL was not verified in this research. No bar-referral phone was found on an official page loaded, so help_phone is null.
polst_name: TPOPP (Transportable Physician Orders for Patient Preferences)
polst_note: Missouri uses TPOPP, a transportable medical order completed with a clinician that records CPR, medical intervention, antibiotic, and nutrition preferences. It does not replace an advance directive, and no official statewide form URL was verified in this research.
proxy_how: Name an attorney in fact in a Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care. The agent may make medical decisions, including decisions about life-prolonging care and disposition of remains, when the person's physician determines they can no longer understand or communicate health care preferences.
proxy_name: Attorney in fact (Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care)

advance_directive_name: Montana My Choices Advance Directive (declaration under the Montana Rights of the Terminally Ill Act)
advance_directive_requirements: Under the Montana Rights of the Terminally Ill Act, MCA Title 50, ch. 9, a directive must be signed by a person at least 18 years old and witnessed by two witnesses. Notarization is not required.
hospice_refusal: A person may direct a physician to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining treatment for an incurable or irreversible condition through a declaration under the Rights of the Terminally Ill Act. Hospice and comfort care are available as end-of-life options.
maid_eligibility: A terminally ill, mentally competent adult patient may request physician aid in dying, and the patient must self-administer the prescribed medication. There is no statute setting out who qualifies; eligibility comes only from the court's decision.
maid_law: Baxter v. Montana, 2009 MT 449 (Montana Supreme Court, decided December 31, 2009)
maid_safeguards: There are no statutory safeguards, steps, or reporting rules, because Montana has no medical aid in dying statute. The court held only that a terminally ill patient's consent is a defense to a homicide charge against the aiding physician under Montana's consent statute.
notes: Medical aid in dying in Montana rests on a court ruling, not a statute, so there is no statutory eligibility list, waiting period, or reporting system. A 2025 bill to remove patient consent as a defense (SB 136) was rejected by the House. Montana also has an End-of-Life Registry run by the Attorney General under MCA § 50-9-501.
polst_note: Montana POLST is a medical order, signed by the patient and a clinician, that records wishes about CPR, medical interventions, and medically assisted nutrition. It is for people near the end of life and does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Name a person to decide about withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment under MCA § 50-9-103, or name a health care agent in a durable health care power of attorney under MCA § 72-5-501. The designee acts when the person is in a terminal condition and can no longer make treatment decisions.
proxy_name: Health care agent (durable health care power of attorney; designee under the Rights of the Terminally Ill Act)

advance_directive_name: Nebraska Advance Health Care Directive (Power of Attorney for Health Care and Living Will Declaration)
advance_directive_requirements: A power of attorney for health care (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 30-3401 to 30-3432) and a living will declaration (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 20-401 to 20-416) must each be signed in front of two adult witnesses or acknowledged before a notary public. Witnesses cannot include the agent, the attending physician, or certain family members and heirs.
hospice_refusal: A person may state in a living will declaration whether life-sustaining procedures, including medically assisted nutrition, should be provided or withheld if they develop a terminal condition and can no longer decide. Hospice care is available as comfort-focused care for terminal illness.
maid_prohibited_note: Nebraska has no medical aid in dying law, and no authorizing statute was found. No prohibiting statute was verified from an official source in this research, so maid_law is null.
notes: Sources conflict on Nebraska's POLST-type form: one source calls it the NETO, while another states Nebraska has no POLST or MOLST statute. The NETO name is reported here with polst_url null. No bar-referral phone was found on an official page loaded, so help_phone is null.
polst_note: Nebraska uses the NETO, a medical order completed with a doctor that records emergency treatment wishes. It does not replace an advance directive, and no official NETO form URL was verified in this research.
proxy_how: Name an attorney-in-fact in a written Power of Attorney for Health Care. The attorney-in-fact may make health care decisions, including decisions about life-sustaining care, when a doctor determines the person cannot make them.
proxy_name: Attorney-in-fact (Power of Attorney for Health Care)

advance_directive_name: Nevada Advance Directive (Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care and Declaration / living will)
advance_directive_requirements: Both parts require either two witnesses or a notary public to sign. The Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care is under NRS 162A.700 to 162A.870, with an optional form at NRS 162A.860; the Declaration is under NRS 449A.433 and must be attested by two witnesses.
hospice_refusal: A person diagnosed with a terminal condition may refuse life-sustaining or life-resuscitating treatment under NRS 449A.400 to 449A.581. A completed advance directive can be filed with the Nevada Secretary of State's Living Will Lockbox for retrieval by providers.
maid_prohibited_note: Nevada has no medical aid in dying law. Assembly Bill 346 (2025) passed the Assembly but died in Senate committee, and Senate Bill 239 (2023) was vetoed by the governor. No prohibiting statute was verified from an official source in this research, so maid_law is null.
notes: No bar-referral phone was found on an official page loaded, so help_phone is null. Nevada also has a separate out-of-hospital Do Not Resuscitate order, which is distinct from POLST.
polst_note: Nevada POLST is a concise medical order completed by a physician, APRN, or physician assistant after discussion with the patient, recording resuscitation orders and three levels of end-of-life interventions. It must be signed by the patient or representative and the clinician, and only health care facilities or providers may order the forms.
proxy_how: Name an adult agent in a Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care. The agent may make medical decisions, including consenting to or refusing treatment and life-sustaining measures, once the person can no longer give informed consent.
proxy_name: Agent (Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care)

advance_directive_name: New Hampshire Advance Directive (Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care and Living Will)
advance_directive_requirements: Under RSA ch. 137-J, with the statutory form at RSA 137-J:20, the advance directive must be signed in front of a notary public or two witnesses. A witness cannot be the person's spouse, agent, a beneficiary of their will, or their physician.
hospice_refusal: RSA 137-J:1 states that all persons have the right to make health care decisions and to refuse health care treatments, including the right to refuse cardiopulmonary resuscitation. A living will gives guidance to an agent, surrogate, and clinicians about life-sustaining treatment.
maid_prohibited_note: New Hampshire has no medical aid in dying law. House Bill 1283 (2024) passed the House but was sent to interim study by the Senate, 17-7, and House Bill 254 (2025) was tabled and did not advance. No prohibiting statute was verified from an official source in this research, so maid_law is null.
notes: No bar-referral phone was found on an official page loaded, so help_phone is null. The living will is guidance; if it conflicts with a durable power of attorney for health care, the power of attorney controls under RSA 137-J:21.
polst_note: New Hampshire law defines POLST at RSA 137-J:2 as a form containing emergency medical orders signed by an attending practitioner, which may include DNR orders. New Hampshire has adopted the national POLST form, and it does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Name an adult agent in the Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care part of the advance directive. The agent may make health care decisions, including decisions about life-sustaining care, when the person lacks capacity to make health care decisions.
proxy_name: Agent (Durable Power of Attorney for Health Care)

advance_directive_name: New Jersey Advance Directive for Health Care (Proxy Directive, Instruction Directive, or Combined Directive)
advance_directive_requirements: Under the New Jersey Advance Directives for Health Care Act, N.J.S.A. 26:2H-53 et seq., an advance directive must be in writing, signed by the person, and witnessed by two adults over 18 or by a notary public. No official advance directive form URL was verified in this research, so advance_directive_url is null.
hospice_refusal: A person may refuse life-sustaining treatment through an advance directive, and hospice care is available as comfort-focused support for terminal illness, usually at home. The Medical Aid in Dying Act does not cover euthanasia or administration of medication by another person.
maid_eligibility: An adult New Jersey resident with capacity to make health care decisions who has been determined by an attending physician and a consulting physician to be terminally ill, with a prognosis of six months or less, may obtain medication to self-administer to end their life.
maid_law: Medical Aid in Dying for the Terminally Ill Act, N.J.S.A. 26:16-1 to -20 (P.L. 2019, c. 59), effective August 1, 2019
maid_safeguards: The patient must make two oral requests at least 15 days apart and one written request on the state form, attested by two witnesses. Only the patient may request the medication; it cannot be requested by a proxy, family member, or through an advance directive, and the patient must self-administer it. Providers and facilities may decline to participate.
notes: The New Jersey Department of Health page confirms the Act is effective as of August 1, 2019. Compliance forms and the Medication Dispensing Record are filed with the Department of Health through the Office of the Chief State Medical Examiner. No bar-referral phone was found on an official page loaded, so help_phone is null.
polst_note: New Jersey POLST is a medical order for seriously ill or medically frail people that records goals of care, CPR, intubation, ventilation, and artificial nutrition preferences. It complements an advance directive, can be completed or amended by a proxy, and does not expire, so it should be reviewed regularly.
proxy_how: Name a health care representative in a Proxy Directive or Combined Directive. The representative may make health care decisions when the person lacks capacity, including decisions to withhold or withdraw life-sustaining treatment in the circumstances the law allows.
